Response to Reviewer #1
Reviewer #1 comments:
This paper describes genome sequencing of a large number of Aspergillus flavus isolates from
across China and a detailed comparative genome analysis of this species through comparing the
new sequences with earlier sequenced genomes. The authors also perform a detailed metabolome
analysis of samples obtained from the isolates and the study represents the most comprehensive
analysis of a single fungal species known today! Considering the importance of A. flavus as a
pathogen and a known producer of mycotoxins the study is extremely valuable, and a particular
interesting finding is the detailed analysis of variations in secondary metabolite production among
the individual strains due to both genetic variations as well as mutations in genes of the
biosynthetic gene clusters. The paper reads very well and presents the results in a clear fashion
and I do not have any comments for improvements. I would just like to congratulate the authors
with such a comprehensive paper.
Response: We would like to express our sincere gratitude to the reviewer for their positive and
encouraging feedback.

Response to Reviewer #2
Reviewer #2 comments:
1. This study presents a large-scale, multi-omics analysis of Aspergillus flavus, integrating
genomics, transcriptomics, and untargeted mass spectrometry-based metabolomics to investigate
phylogeographic patterns and regulatory drivers of specialized metabolism. The manuscript
provides valuable insights into fungal secondary metabolite diversity and proposes connections
between biosynthetic gene clusters (BGCs), environmental origin, and metabolic output. Given
the growing interest in microbial metabolomics in ecological and evolutionary research, the work
is timely and potentially impactful.
Response: We would like to express our sincere gratitude for your constructive comments, which
highlighted the significant aspects of our research. Your comments have been encouraging and have
motivated us to continue our efforts to improve our study.
2.However, several critical aspects of the mass spectrometry methodology (particularly related to
signal-to-noise thresholds, gap filling practices, metabolite identification confidence, and dataset
merging) require clarification and improvement to enhance the reproducibility and
interpretability of the results. Major Revisions.
Response: Thank you for your very helpful comments, which have enabled us to significantly improve
the quality of the manuscript. We agree with the reviewers’ comments and requests and have added
analyses and results to support our feature finding, annotation workflow, and results. We clarified and
improved the key deficiencies in the mass spectrometry method raised by the reviewers. These indicated
issues have been addressed in accordance with the reviewers' comments, and we respond to the points
one by one in detail below.
L910. The authors report on using an MS2 noise threshold of 100 intensity units (1E2) in the
MZmine feature processing workflow. This threshold is unusually permissive for high-resolution
Orbitrap data, where baseline noise in complex biological matrices (e.g., fungal extracts) typically
exceeds this value. The inclusion of such low-intensity fragment ions increases the likelihood of
incorporating noise-derived or non-informative peaks, which can degrade the quality of MS/MS
spectra. This setting undermines the reliability of spectral similarity scores and increases the risk
of false-positive annotations, spurious molecular networking connections, and diminished
reproducibility. The authors are strongly encouraged to reprocess the data using a more stringent
MS2 noise threshold (≥1E3–1E4), as recommended for Orbitrap-based untargeted metabolomics
(Mahieu and Patti, 2017).
Response: Thanks to the reviewer for raising this point. We agree with the reviewer's comments and
recognize the concern that too low a threshold for MS2 noise may lead to inaccurate metabolite
identification. We follow the reviewers' suggestions and raised the MS2 noise threshold from E2 to 6E3.
To better justify the chosen parameter settings, the final MS2 noise threshold (6E3) selection was
determined by comparing the number of core and unique metabolites identified with the GNPS platform
through Feature-Based Molecular Networking (FBMN) analysis across eight preset MS2 thresholds
(1E0; 1E2; 1E3; 2E3; 4E3; 6E3; 8E3; 1E4) in the MS2 peak detection step, mostly falling within the
recommended Orbitrap-based untargeted metabolomics MS2 noise threshold range (≥1E3–1E4)1. To
facilitate reviewers in viewing the MS/MS spectra and quantitative matrix tables extracted at different
MS2 noise thresholds, we have uploaded analysis results to Google Drive
(https://drive.google.com/drive/folders/1dD04vMPQ8pYAHq87mubIPPowUvpJdn-
h?dmr=1&ec=wgc-drive-globalnav-goto). In this parameter optimization analysis, except for the MS2
noise threshold, all other parameters were kept equal. The metabolome batch processing workflow for
544 samples in MZmine 4 is shown in Re_Figure 1a. We used optimized mass spectrometry acquisition
parameters in the data acquisition method2, including the AGC value, the high-energy collision-induced
dissociation (HCD). The intensity filtering parameter (MS1=1E5, in this study) between the MS1
acquisition and the MS2 acquisition part was set. Only those precursor ions with MS1 features greater
than the threshold will be fragmented into MS2 product ions by the high-energy collision-induced
dissociation (HCD). Thanks to the high selectivity and sensitivity of HPLC-Orbitrap Fusion-MS, we
obtained relatively clean MS/MS spectra. In the FBMN analysis, the cosine similarity score threshold
was set to 0.6, and the minimum number of MS2 spectra matching data points between the sample and
reference spectra was 6. Other detailed analysis procedures and parameters in mzmine 4.29 are
explained in the Methods section.
Re_Figure 1| a. Mzmine 4 analyzes batch processing in a streamlined analysis mode, and the gap-
filling step includes four filtering steps: the intensity tolerance (20%), mz/ tolerance (sample-to-sample),
retention time, and minimum scans (data points) filtering steps.
We observed a decrease in metabolic features containing MS/MS spectra with increasing MS2
noise threshold (Re_Figure 2a). For example, we observe a decrease of annotated metabolites (n=371-
335=36) when increasing the MS2 noise threshold from 1E2 to 1E4, and as the MS2 noise threshold
increases, the number of identified metabolites further decreases (Re_Figure 2b). In particular, the
previously set MS2 noise threshold (1E2) had ~15% ((371-317)/371=~15%) identified metabolites that
may carry a high risk of false positives, as these were not consequently annotated (Re_Figure 2c). 317
annotated metabolites were identified under all MS2 noise threshold conditions without gap-filling
treatment, accounting for ~85% (317/371). Based on the above threshold comparison analysis results,
we made a trade-off between the number of identified metabolites and reliability and decided to use the
6E3 threshold.
Re_Figure 2| a. The number of extracted metabolic features/MS2 spectra by Feature-Based Molecular
Networking (FBMN) analysis across seven preset MS2 thresholds, with or without a gap-filling step. b.
The number of identified metabolites by Feature-Based Molecular Networking (FBMN) analysis across
seven preset MS2 thresholds with or without a gap-filling steps. c. Venn diagram showing the
intersection and union of metabolites identified by FBMN analysis at seven MS2 noise threshold
settings without gap-filling step. c. Venn diagram showing the intersection and union of metabolites
identified by FBMN analysis at seven MS2 noise threshold settings with a gap-filling step.
After determining the most critical MS2 noise threshold in metabolite identification, we identified
metabolite MS/MS spectra by aligning with the MS/MS spectra in reference database based on three
metabolite identification platforms (annotation Level 2). These platforms include: (1) FBMN from the
GNPS metabolomics analysis environment. The FBMN analysis results after increasing the MS/MS
extraction threshold to 6E3 were performed on the GNPS platform and the results were stored in GNPS
website (https://gnps.ucsd.edu/ProteoSAFe/status.jsp?task=1d02472cebf54e63999ee7c0d7891a5d); (2)
Compound Discovery, an online or offline metabolomics analysis software from the instrument
manufacturer Thermo Fisher, which compares to mzCloud, a database built using 32,330 standards by
Thermo Fisher (Data as of October 2025 for https://www.mzcloud.org/). The metabolite identification
analysis results of Compound Discovery are listed in the supplementary material table; and (3)
MetDNA3, which primarily identifies primary metabolites in this study. The annotation results of
MetDNA3 are presented in the supplementary material table 10; Furthermore, on top of these large mass
spectral libraries, for the aflatoxin biosynthesis pathway, representing key metabolites of interest in this
study, we previously developed a targeted metabolite monitoring method. In our previous study, 12
MS/MS spectra of standards for compounds in the aflatoxin biosynthesis pathway were collected3. We
uploaded 355 metabolites MS/MS spectral alignment mirror plots to demonstrate the reliability of the
metabolites annotation results through corresponding matches of higher-abundant mass fragments
together with high cosine similarity scores of the spectral match. The mirror plots are stored in
https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/_b_554AFs_1E56E3_no_gap-filling_Mirror_plot_b_/30434335.
Since Figshare website does not provide a convenient way to view mirror plots, we have selected eight
metabolites and displayed their mirror plots below (Re_Figure 3).
Re_Figure 3| The mirror plots of 8 metabolites. The black portion at the top is the MS/MS spectrum
from the sample, and the green portion at the bottom is the MS/MS spectrum from the GNPS library.
The mirror graph includes the cosine similarity score.
L920. The use of gap filling to address missing features further compounds the concern raised
above. Although gap filling is widely accepted to mitigate missing values caused by stochastic MS2
sampling in DDA workflows, it can introduce false-positive intensities, particularly when applied
to features near the noise threshold. In this study, the permissive MS2 threshold amplifies this
risk, increasing the probability that baseline fluctuations or background ions are retrospectively
integrated as genuine peaks. The authors should clarify how gap-filled features were treated in
downstream analyses and whether any filtering based on reproducibility or detection frequency
was applied.
Response: We agree with the reviewer's comments and appreciate the suggestions to improve the
quality of our manuscript. As the reviewer was concerned about, using gap filling with a low MS2 noise
threshold to address missing features exacerbates the issues raised regarding false-positive annotations,
spurious molecular networking connections, and reduced reproducibility (impacting qualitative analysis
results), as well as leading to false-positive intensities (impacting quantitative analysis results). As
indicated above, following the reviewer's suggestion, we increased the MS2 noise threshold to 6E3 to
address these concerns. We evaluated the effects of a gap-filling step on the qualitative and quantitative
metabolite analysis results. We will next describe the comparative evaluation results in detail, clarifying
how gap-filled features were treated in downstream analyses and the frequency with which they were
detected.
Firstly, we added a set of analyses on the effect of gap-filling on metabolite qualitative analysis
when performing MS2 noise threshold parameter optimization analysis experiments. We found that the
MS2 noise threshold should be increased to at least 2E3 to affect the change of the MS/MS spectrum
for this dataset. The gap-filling treatment reduced the number of MS1 features, MS/MS spectra, and
identified metabolites, and as the MS2 noise threshold increased, the trend of the number of identified
metabolites was similar to that without the gap-filling step (Re_Figure 2a,b). Importantly, the difference
in the number of MS/MS spectra reduced by adding the gap-filling step is much greater than the
difference in the number of MS/MS spectra reduced by changing the MS2 noise threshold (Re_Figure
2a,b,c,d). We also observed that almost all metabolites identified (99%) in the gap-filling treatment
were also identified in the treatment without gap-filling (Re_Figure 4). In the export step parameter
settings, we only export metabolic features with MS2, so the number of MS1 features and the number
of MS/MS spectra are the same (Re_Figure 2a). We speculate that adding a gap-filling step increases
the intensity tolerance, mz/tolerance (sample-to-sample), retention time, and minimum scans (data
points) filtering steps (Re_Figure 1a), thereby reducing the number of MS/MS spectra we obtain and
thus leading to a decrease in the number of identified metabolites. So, adding a gap-filling step increases
the data quality of the MS/MS spectra, but it may also filter out the specialized metabolites, such as
Aflatoxin G2, Aflatoxin M1, and Aflatrem, that are produced by a small number of strains we are
interested in this study (Re_Figure 4). In summary, it is a matter of choice: with additional filters in
“Feature finder” steps, we may (and do) end up with fewer features, but they may be of higher data
quality for the feature matrix. Also, the gap filling may help to get better statistics downstream, but it
may also yield artifacts due to the added minimal values (Re_Figure 2a,b). We upload the MS/MS
alignment mirror plot of these metabolites in
https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/_b_554AFs_1E56E3_no_gap-filling_Mirror_plot_b_/30434335.
Re_Figure 4| Adding a gap-filling step can lead to the loss of useful MS/MS spectra information,
thereby reducing the number of metabolites of interest identified, for example, Aflatrem.
In addition, a dilemma arises from comparing the Aspergillus metabolites in the Natural Products
Atlas (https://www.npatlas.org/), CMMAspergillusDB
(https://github.com/albertogilf/ceuMassMediator/tree/master/CMMAspergillusDB), and Reaxys
(https://www.reaxys.com), three microbial natural product databases, with the current microbial natural
product platform, GNPS, which utilizes MS/MS spectra. It was found that a large proportion of
Aspergillus metabolites lack MS/MS spectra. This situation has been reflected in several other studies
of fungal secondary metabolites. For example, in the recent article on an A. flavus population published
in PNAS4, putative MS/MS spectra of 13 secondary metabolites were provided in the supplementary
materials. However, only 4 metabolites in this study belonged to the annotation level 2 (annotated by
GNPS), and 9 metabolites did not show the comparison results of the MS/MS spectra of the samples
and the MS/MS spectra of the standards/ reference database (mirror plot). Instead, they were identified
by searching the MS1 accurate mass (±5 ppm) and isotope pattern information in the PubChem database
(annotation level 3). PubChem lacked MS/MS spectral information for these metabolites. Another effort
recently studied the diversity of the cyclopiazonic acid family of mycotoxins in A. flavus by UHPLC
Triple-TOF HRMS5. In this study, the authors collected 30 CPA-type alkaloids previously isolated and
identified from Aspergillus genus strains by natural product researchers. They compiled their molecular
formulas and exact mass (MS1, ±5 ppm) data and then identified 22 members of the cyclopiazonic acid
family from the A. flavus strains extracts using UHPLC Triple-TOF HRMS. The authors also provided
MS/MS spectra and putative structural fragments for 22 detected secondary metabolites. We decided to
use a similar approach as followed by other natural product researchers and used MS1 (±3 ppm) and
species origin information to annotate by matching an in-house Aspergillus metabolite list (n= 6796)
extracted from CMMAspergillusDB6, NPAtlas7, and Reaxys. In addition, some MS/MS spectra also
exist in the literature, but they are not included in the GNPS library. We also performed in-silico
annotation of the MS/MS spectra through Sirius8,9, MolDiscovery10and DEREPLICATOR+11, making
use of the assembled metabolite list. Finally, we compared MS/MS spectra in the literature with the
characteristic ions in the MS/MS spectra of our samples for metabolites annotation. We define these
identified metabolites as annotation level 3 in this study. Although they are not as reliable as level 2
metabolites, we believe they still have a sufficient degree of credibility to make them worth reporting.
Tools for performing MS1 matching tasks can prepare in-house databases, and then the tools of MZmine
412, TidyMass13, and Compound Discovery 3 (Thermo Fisher, USA) be used to annotate experimental
data. For example, the following is a schematic diagram of the process of performing MS1 metabolite
annotation using the metID component in TidyMass (Re_Figure 5). We then verified the metabolites
with annotation level 3 in Xcalibur to ensure their presence in the quality control samples and strain
samples. Finally, 195 specialized (secondary) metabolites (annotation level 3) were mapped using
Compound Discovery 3 and an in-house Aspergillus metabolites list (n= 4799), and we then manually
inspected them in Xcalibur 4.0 and selected 46 annotation level 3 and 14 annotation level 2 from GNPS
to study their differential abundance across samples. This metabolite abundance matrix is provided in
the Supplementary Table 15, and the MS/MS spectra of these metabolites are provided in the
Supplementary Material Figures 18-26.
Re_Figure 5| A schematic diagram of the process of performing three metabolite annotation levels using
the metID component in TidyMass13.
In terms of quantification, after weighing the pros and cons, we decided to perform quantification
in two parts. We set the MS2 noise threshold at 6E3 and conduct metabolome analysis to obtain a gap-
filled features matrix for downstream analysis (Supplementary Materials Table 14). For the part of
metabolites identified by GNPS, MetDNA3 and Compound Discovery (n=306+87+85=478, >= level
2), a 30% detection frequency filter was applied. It is well known that an 80% detection frequency filter
rule is popular in focusing on intergroup differences in metabolomics studies, for example, clinical
metabolomics, where researchers expect more similar samples/sample matrices to ensure consistency
between biological replicates. However, given that we are also interested in specialized metabolites that
are produced by a small number of strains from different ecological environments, we put this filter
lower, i.e., 30% at the beginning of the current study. After this detection frequency filtering (>=30%
samples) and manual deduplication, 260 metabolites remained (>= level 2) for subsequent multi-group
differential analysis to find metabolites specific to different populations. However, among these 260
metabolites (>= level 2), only a small number of specialized metabolites (n=6) isolated from A. flavus
can be matched one-to-one with the predicted and annotated biosynthetic gene cluster (BGCs) of the A.
flavus genome (predicted secondary metabolites) by antiSMASH (fungal version) with matches to the
MIBiG database and 16 secondary metabolite biosynthetic pathways14 that have been experimentally
elucidated in A. flavus. These are Aflatoxin B , Aflatoxin B , Cyclopiazonic acid, O-
1 2
Methylsterigmatocystin, Sterigmatocystin, and Ferrichrysin. However, although we identified Aflatoxin
G1, Aflatoxin G2, Alternariol, Penicillin G, and Aflatrem using GNPS (without gap-filling treatment),
they were filtered out due to their low occurrence in the samples (<30% samples). It can be seen that
using only gap-filling treatment will lead to the loss of some secondary metabolite information of
interest. For annotation levels 2 and 3 of A. flavus secondary metabolites with a detection frequency of
less than 30%, we manually semi-quantified the target metabolites' intensity using the quantitation
browser in the instrument manufacturer's Xcalibur 4.0 software (similar to a targeted metabolomics
analysis strategy). This peak intensity detection method is more accurate than high-throughput non-
targeted peak detection, such as the one used in MZmine. If we find that the starting point or end point
of some mass spectrometry peaks is not calculated correctly, we will manually select the starting and
ending points of each mass spectrometry peak to capture a more accurate peak area. This metabolite
intensity matrix is provided in the supplementary table 15.
Next, according to the input file format requirements of MetaboAnalyst, we added the sample
metadata information to the metabolite peak table matrix. 260 metabolite matrices filtered by 30%
detection frequency (MS2 noise threshold=6E3 and with gap-filling treatment, annotation level 2) and
60 manually semi-quantitative secondary metabolite matrices (MS2 noise threshold=6E3 and without
gap-filling treatment, annotation level 2 or 3) will be imported into the metabolomics statistical analysis
platform MetaboAnalyst15 to perform metabolomics data matrix preprocessing and multivariate
statistical analysis. Detailed data preprocessing steps: 1. The data filtering step is omitted because we
have already filtered the 260 metabolite data matrices. The 60 manually semi-quantitative secondary

normalization, select Normalization by sum; . Data transformation, select Log transformation (base

The data normalization results show that the intensities of 260 annotated metabolites changed from a
skewed distribution before normalization to a nearly normal distribution after normalization. 3.
Subsequently, multivariate statistical analysis has been performed. We chose the PLS-DA differential
analysis algorithm to perform multi-group comparative analysis of different clades to determine the
differentiation patterns of different metabolites. We compared the intensity distribution of Aflatoxin B
1

and the distribution of Aflatoxin B detected manually using Xcalibur semi-quantitative analysis (Re-
2, 4, 5, and 6 was high, especially Chinese clade 4, which was the highest and a high-toxin-producing
subgroup. The two data processing methods had high consistency.
Finally, the secondary metabolites data matrix (supplementary table 15) used in the modified
Figure 2b, Figure 4a, and Figure 6a of the manuscript was manually checked using Xcalibur to ensure
that the metabolites had reliable intensity values for semi-quantification. The metabolite intensity data
matrix used in Figure 7 of the manuscript uses the gap-filled data matrix (supplementary table 14) was
preprocessed and then subjected to multivariate statistical analysis, for example, PLS-DA.

L924. The manuscript describes the fusion of MS1-only data from Drott et al. with the authors’
own MS1/MS2-rich dataset. This reviewer finds this practice debatable. Without MS/MS data, no
structural confirmation is possible, and without retention time alignment or adduct correction,
accurate mass alone is insufficient for robust feature matching. This approach violates standard
and well-published practices in cross-dataset untargeted metabolomics integration and raises
significant concerns about false feature merging and annotation bias (Dunn et al., 2011;
Broadhurst et al., 2018). The authors should, at minimum, report the m/z tolerance window used
for matching, whether adduct species were deconvoluted, and how annotation uncertainty was
handled during matrix fusion.
Response: We are grateful to the reviewer for pointing out this issue. The dataset created by our co-
author, Dr. Drott, was reanalyzed according to the reviewer's comments, and the two datasets were fused
according to the minimum requirements1,16 recommended by the reviewer. Previously, we only utilized
quantitative data containing MS1, but did not include the files containing MS/MS spectrum information
for qualitative analysis. We have now uploaded the 24 qualitative files containing the MS/MS mass
spectra to the GNPS repository. The updated LC-MS/MS 24 qualitative files (12 positive and 12
negative files) are now available through the MassIVE repository (ID no. MSV000087134,
https://doi.org/doi:10.25345/C54226). They used a target method of PRM mode acquired the data on
the Thermo Scientific Q Exactive Orbitrap mass spectrometer. For the 94 USA strain samples, MS1
information had been acquired for quantification, and then qualitative files were collected to acquire the
MS/MS spectral information for a targeted set of compounds. The previous PNAS-published effort
studied 13 experimentally verified pathways for specialized (or secondary) metabolites, but did not
study those pathways that have been isolated and identified in A. flavus but whose corresponding
unknown BGCs have not yet been resolved. The identification of 13 metabolites was completed by Tom
ás and Drott and they provided MS/MS spectra information of 13 secondary metabolites in the PNAS
article4 (Table S4 and SI Appendix, Figs. S5–S29 in this article). Four of the specialized metabolites
(SMs) belong to annotation level 2, and the other nine metabolites belong to annotation level 3.
Previously, we merged the metabolite quantification table with our data matrix based on the MS1
accurate mass (±5 ppm, m/z tolerance window) (annotation level 3). However, this data fusion method
comes with risks, as pointed out by the reviewers. Therefore, we performed MS1 and MS2 detection
using the mzmine 4 workflow and FBMN analysis on the updated files containing MS/MS data with
the same parameters, aiming to merge the two datasets based on MS1 accurate mass (±5 ppm, m/z
tolerance window) and MS/MS spectrum comparison results (annotation level 2). We only retained the
MS1 metabolic features that had MS/MS spectra. From the mzmine analysis results, we can see that
Drott et.al’s dataset contains MS/MS spectral information on hundreds of metabolites, which is
consistent with their goal of targeting the analysis of a few SMs (Re_Figure 8). However, compared
with the number of MS1 spectra reported in their PNAS article4 (Fig 2A in this article), the number of
metabolic features (MS1) containing MS/MS spectra is small. Therefore, it is difficult to perform FBMN
joint analysis with our dataset, rich in MS/MS spectra information. We therefore performed a separate
FBMN analysis and only matched 3 metabolites with the GNPS reference library, including aflatoxin
B , cyclopiazonic acid, and aflatrem (GNPS job result link:
1
https://gnps.ucsd.edu/ProteoSAFe/status.jsp?task=3532f01f1f8a47c9b2e36eca093b89bc). This is
consistent with the results of annotation level 2 shown in Table S4 in their PNAS4 article (annotation
level 2), except for the metabolite Ditryptophenaline. Furthermore, we did not find the
Ditryptophenaline MS/MS spectrum in the GNPS library. Although we identified aflatrem in our dataset,
the metabolite was present at low concentration levels (MS1 peak intensity less than 1E5) under the
culture conditions we used, and it was not detected in most samples. The dataset created by Drott used
two different culture media. In order to comply with the minimum standards proposed by the reviewers,
we therefore selected two A. flavus secondary metabolites including Aflatoxin B (cosine similarity
1
score=0.99) and Cyclopiazonic acid (cosine similarity score=0.96) for data fusion (±5ppm, m/z
tolerance window, and with MS/MS spectrum alignment mirror plot ) to verify that the presence/absence
variation of the BGC gene in the strains from China and the United States in our manuscript can only
partially explain the changes in specialized metabolites. The results still support our conclusions
(updated Figure 4a and Figure S8). The fact that the pattern of BGC variation can only partially explain
the changes in SMs has thus been demonstrated in the two BGC-SM pairs for aflatoxin B and
Re_Figure 8| Metabolic features and number of MS/MS spectra extracted from mass spectrometry data
from Drott’s database under different MS1 and MS2 noise thresholds.
L932. The authors state that metabolite identification was performed using an in-house mycotoxin
library of over 260 compounds, with confirmation based on accurate mass (±5 ppm), MS/MS
spectra, retention time, and isotope pattern. However, no evidence is provided (such as GNPS
molecular networking results, mirror plots, or cosine similarity scores) to support the claim of
Level 1 or Level 2 identifications. This omission limits the reviewer’s ability to verify structural
assignments. The authors should provide: GNPS job links (not currently listed in L945–953),
representative mirror plots showing MS/MS spectral matches between standards and samples,
and cosine similarity metrics for key annotated compounds. Without these supporting materials,
the claim of confirmed identification using authentic standards remains unsubstantiated.
Response: We thank the reviewer for pointing out this key omission. As requested by the reviewers, we
provide the GNPS job links (6E3 MS2 noise threshold results:
https://gnps.ucsd.edu/ProteoSAFe/status.jsp?task=9bcbcfc1ba7945a887c8b4a418265b97) and mirror
plots generated by GNPS in our dataset in the manuscript (The figshare links:
https://figshare.com/articles/dataset/_b_554AFs_1E56E3_no_gap-filling_Mirror_plot_b_/30434335).
The in-house mycotoxin database contains the following mycotoxins produced by the species
Aspergillus flavus: Aflatoxin B , Aflatoxin B , Aflatoxin G , Aflatoxin G , Aflatoxin M , Aflatoxin M,
1 2 1 2 1 2
O-Methylsterigmatocystin, 11-hydroxy O-methylsterigmatocystin (HOMST), Sterigmatocystin, 5-
methoxysterigmatocystin, Versicolorin A, Versicolorin B, versiconol, Tenuazonic acid,
Ditryptophenaline, and Kojic acid. We selected four aflatoxin pathway-related metabolites and
presented their MS/MS alignment results (Re-Figure 9, Level 1). Our laboratory is a national biotoxin

been collected, and we established a mycotoxins mass spectrometry database. Some of the standards are

highly reproducible (Re-Figure 10). We also then selected two metabolites for peak alignment and
found that the peaks exhibited excellent reproducibility, demonstrating the robustness of our
chromatographic method when analyzing different samples (Re-Figure 11). The robustness and
reproducibility of peak intensity are crucial for quantitative results.

Include any potential limitations related to mass spectrometry and metabolomics data analysis in
the discussion section. Also, the authors should ensure that mass spectrometry-related
terminology is consistently and correctly formatted throughout the manuscript. For example, the
mass-to-charge ratio should be written as m/z (in italics and with a lowercase "m") following
standard conventions. Please review the text to correct any inconsistencies in the formatting of
this and related terms.
Response: We would like to thank the reviewer for their valuable comments. In the Discussion section,
as requested, we have added the potential limitations related to mass spectrometry and metabolomics
data analysis, as well as our future effort directions. Specifically: “Under the currently used medium
culture conditions, metabolite structures of nine of the sixteen experimentally resolved biosynthetic
gene clusters (BGCs) could be identified in the metabolome data. We note that a single culture condition
(universal PDA medium here) is unlikely to be sufficient to describe the comprehensive specialized
metabolic diversity of fungi, as a significant proportion of BGCs are typically inactive and require
specific conditions to be activated, expressed, and biosynthesized17,18. Our pan-transcriptome analysis
of 28 strains from different subpopulations under the same culture conditions validated that a large
proportion of BGC genes were expressed at low levels or not at all (Supplementary Table 6).
Alternatively, limitations in extraction solvents (the protocol used here does not include dedicated
lipidome extraction solvents) and separation conditions (e.g., HILIC column for polar metabolites) may
have prevented the detection of additional metabolites. In terms of mass spectrometry methods, adopting
both DDA (Data-Dependent Acquisition) and DIA (Data-Independent Acquisition) data acquisition
modes could facilitate the identification of more metabolites. In metabolomics data analysis, newly
developed AI-driven methods such as MassCube19, MS2Query20, Flash Entropy Search21, and the
Spectral Denoising Search22 may enhance both the number and accuracy of metabolite annotations,
surpassing traditional cosine similarity-based alignment algorithms. Currently, many fungal metabolites
that have been isolated and identified, however, still lack high-quality MS/MS spectral information in
public databases, which limits the number of specialized metabolites we can identify.”
We also appreciate the reviewers' suggestions and have consistently and correctly formatted the
mass spectrometry-related terminology terms such as “m/z”, throughout the manuscript, as requested by
the reviewers.
Conclusion
The integration of omics layers in this study is conceptually strong, and the manuscript addresses
a highly relevant biological question. However, multiple issues in the mass spectrometry data
processing pipeline and metabolite annotation framework require careful revision. Addressing
these concerns will significantly strengthen the manuscript’s technical foundation and improve its
reproducibility and impact.
Response: We thank the reviewers for their expert review of our manuscript and for their positive
feedback and affirmation of its merits. We optimized and adjusted the parameter thresholds as requested
by the reviewers and reanalyzed the untargeted metabolomics data. Multiple issues in the mass
spectrometry data processing pipeline and metabolite annotation framework have been carefully revised
one by one. This greatly improved the quality of our manuscript and the clarity of our results.

The pangenome was determined based on “567 representative genomes” (line 252). Unless I
missed it, it is not explained in the corresponding section of the material and methods how these
567 genomes were representatively selected. This has implications for the use of the rarefaction
curve in Figure 3b, for example. If the 567 genomes comprised the 544 newly-sequenced Chinese
genomes plus some additionals, then this is hardly a representative set.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewers for pointing out these concerns. The pan-genome
constructed from the genomes of the previous 567 strains did indeed suffer from insufficient sample
representation. Therefore, following the reviewers' suggestions, we reassembled and annotated 410 new
strains from previously published data using the same pipeline, and then constructed a new pan-genome
comprising 977 strains. The genomes of about 75 strains in 1051 strains were filtered out due to issues
such as low assembly quality. These 977 strains cover 9 countries, including 75 clinical strains23 and
902 environmental strains isolated from soil, peanuts, corn, cotton, and other sources4,24. We hope that
the current edition of the pangenome is representative of the available A. flavus genome globally. We
added a column for "Pangenome samples" to the strain metadata table in the supplementary materials
table 1 to label the samples used for pangenome construction. In fact, we constructed three versions of
the A.flavus pangenome, starting with 259 strains from China (Re-Figure 22a), increasing to 567 (Re-
Figure 22b), and now reaching 977 strains (Re-Figure 22c). In the second edition of the pan-genome
analysis, we did indeed primarily analyze samples from China (n=539), and also selected 28 strains
genomes from different geographical environments from NCBI. This version of the pangenome does
not include clinical samples and strains from a wider range of environmental sources. We therefore re-
assembled and annotated 410 strains from previously published data, then constructed a new pan-
genome comprising 977 strains. Following this pangenome construction, we performed rigorous
bacterial sequence decontamination analysis by aligning the NR database. We did not perform a rigorous
decontamination step during the pangenome construction process of 567 strains version. Therefore, the
total number of genes in the previously submitted pangenome was 16,416, while the actual number after
decontamination was 15,035. Compared to the pangenome constructed using 567 strains, the
pangenome constructed using 977 samples increased in size by 2.58 Mb and added 647 genes. We found
that as the genome size increases, the pangenome size and the number of predicted genes also increase,
but the increase is relatively small, unlike in prokaryotes. It is evident that although the number of
genome samples increased by 410, the number of genes increased only slightly. Orthology inference
revealed that the A. flavus pangenome is composed of 15,628 protein-coding genes, which is 3,181
genes more than the reference genome of A.flavus NRRL3357 (GCA_009017415.1)25. These non-
redundant orthogroups could be subdivided into core (in all isolates, n = 9,584), accessory (in 5-95%
of the isolates, n = 5,085) and ‘unique’ (in <5% of the isolates, n = 959) genomes (Fig. 3a) after rigorous
removal of bacterial and other prokaryotic sequences by aligning the NR database. Here we need to
correct an analysis error in our previously submitted manuscript. Among them, the conserved core
genome accounts for 61.3%, the accessory genome accounts for 32.5%, and the unique genes account
for the remaining 6.2% of genes. The pangenome exhibits a closed trend as the population size increases
(Fig. 3b). Further results regarding the pangenome were updated in the manuscript.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
This letter is to inform you that after carefully reviewing the current and corrected version of the manuscript entitled "Large-Scale Multi-Omics Profiling Reveals Environmental and Evolutionary Drivers in Phylogeographic Diversity of Fungal Specialized Metabolism", I’m very glad to express that the authors have addressed my major concerns (metabolomics component of the study) in a thorough, transparent, and technically rigorous manner. This new version of the manuscript substantially improves the reliability and reproducibility of metabolomics analysis, which was the central focus of my earlier critique.

Below, I summarize my assessment:
1. The authors corrected the overly permissive MS2 noise threshold (originally 1E2) and performed a systematic optimization across a wide range of thresholds. The selection of 6E3 is well justified based on comparative feature counts, metabolite overlap, and annotation stability. There is no more concern about this as presented in the current version.
2. The authors performed a detailed comparison with and without gap filling, demonstrating: the impact on MS/MS feature counts, the risk of losing uncommon specialized metabolites, the effect on downstream quantification, and how gap-filled versus manually quantified data were separated in analysis. They now clearly describe how gap-filled features are treated and filtered, and this response is acceptable and demonstrates a solid understanding of the tradeoffs.
3. Regarding the dataset fusion with MS1-only used from Drott et al. The authors state now using MS/MS files and even uploading 24 qualitative files to the GNPS repository. The integration is now performed according to minimal acceptable standards for cross-dataset untargeted metabolomics analysis. This adequately resolves my concern.
4. In case of the metabolite identification confidence levels (Level 1, Level 2), the authors provided the corresponding GNPS job links, as well as retention time comparisons with authentic standards, cosine similarity metrics, chromatographic evidence, and the identification framework is now transparent and appropriately supported. This is a major improvement and fully satisfies my request.
5. The authors now acknowledge important limitations, including single culture conditions, inactive BGCs, and incomplete fungal MS/MS coverage in public databases, among others. These additions provide a more realistic frame of the metabolomics results.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3: The authors have sufficiently (and in high detail) addressed the comments that I raised.
