Include any potential limitations related to mass spectrometry and metabolomics data analysis in
the discussion section. Also, the authors should ensure that mass spectrometry-related
terminology is consistently and correctly formatted throughout the manuscript. For example, the
mass-to-charge ratio should be written as m/z (in italics and with a lowercase "m") following
standard conventions. Please review the text to correct any inconsistencies in the formatting of
this and related terms.
Response: We would like to thank the reviewer for their valuable comments. In the Discussion section,
as requested, we have added the potential limitations related to mass spectrometry and metabolomics
data analysis, as well as our future effort directions. Specifically: “Under the currently used medium
culture conditions, metabolite structures of nine of the sixteen experimentally resolved biosynthetic
gene clusters (BGCs) could be identified in the metabolome data. We note that a single culture condition
(universal PDA medium here) is unlikely to be sufficient to describe the comprehensive specialized
metabolic diversity of fungi, as a significant proportion of BGCs are typically inactive and require
specific conditions to be activated, expressed, and biosynthesized17,18. Our pan-transcriptome analysis
of 28 strains from different subpopulations under the same culture conditions validated that a large
proportion of BGC genes were expressed at low levels or not at all (Supplementary Table 6).
Alternatively, limitations in extraction solvents (the protocol used here does not include dedicated
lipidome extraction solvents) and separation conditions (e.g., HILIC column for polar metabolites) may
have prevented the detection of additional metabolites. In terms of mass spectrometry methods, adopting
both DDA (Data-Dependent Acquisition) and DIA (Data-Independent Acquisition) data acquisition
modes could facilitate the identification of more metabolites. In metabolomics data analysis, newly
developed AI-driven methods such as MassCube19, MS2Query20, Flash Entropy Search21, and the
Spectral Denoising Search22 may enhance both the number and accuracy of metabolite annotations,
surpassing traditional cosine similarity-based alignment algorithms. Currently, many fungal metabolites
that have been isolated and identified, however, still lack high-quality MS/MS spectral information in
public databases, which limits the number of specialized metabolites we can identify.”
We also appreciate the reviewers' suggestions and have consistently and correctly formatted the
mass spectrometry-related terminology terms such as “m/z”, throughout the manuscript, as requested by
the reviewers.
Conclusion
The integration of omics layers in this study is conceptually strong, and the manuscript addresses
a highly relevant biological question. However, multiple issues in the mass spectrometry data
processing pipeline and metabolite annotation framework require careful revision. Addressing
these concerns will significantly strengthen the manuscript’s technical foundation and improve its
reproducibility and impact.
Response: We thank the reviewers for their expert review of our manuscript and for their positive
feedback and affirmation of its merits. We optimized and adjusted the parameter thresholds as requested
by the reviewers and reanalyzed the untargeted metabolomics data. Multiple issues in the mass
spectrometry data processing pipeline and metabolite annotation framework have been carefully revised
one by one. This greatly improved the quality of our manuscript and the clarity of our results.

The pangenome was determined based on “567 representative genomes” (line 252). Unless I
missed it, it is not explained in the corresponding section of the material and methods how these
567 genomes were representatively selected. This has implications for the use of the rarefaction
curve in Figure 3b, for example. If the 567 genomes comprised the 544 newly-sequenced Chinese
genomes plus some additionals, then this is hardly a representative set.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewers for pointing out these concerns. The pan-genome
constructed from the genomes of the previous 567 strains did indeed suffer from insufficient sample
representation. Therefore, following the reviewers' suggestions, we reassembled and annotated 410 new
strains from previously published data using the same pipeline, and then constructed a new pan-genome
comprising 977 strains. The genomes of about 75 strains in 1051 strains were filtered out due to issues
such as low assembly quality. These 977 strains cover 9 countries, including 75 clinical strains23 and
902 environmental strains isolated from soil, peanuts, corn, cotton, and other sources4,24. We hope that
the current edition of the pangenome is representative of the available A. flavus genome globally. We
added a column for "Pangenome samples" to the strain metadata table in the supplementary materials
table 1 to label the samples used for pangenome construction. In fact, we constructed three versions of
the A.flavus pangenome, starting with 259 strains from China (Re-Figure 22a), increasing to 567 (Re-
Figure 22b), and now reaching 977 strains (Re-Figure 22c). In the second edition of the pan-genome
analysis, we did indeed primarily analyze samples from China (n=539), and also selected 28 strains
genomes from different geographical environments from NCBI. This version of the pangenome does
not include clinical samples and strains from a wider range of environmental sources. We therefore re-
assembled and annotated 410 strains from previously published data, then constructed a new pan-
genome comprising 977 strains. Following this pangenome construction, we performed rigorous
bacterial sequence decontamination analysis by aligning the NR database. We did not perform a rigorous
decontamination step during the pangenome construction process of 567 strains version. Therefore, the
total number of genes in the previously submitted pangenome was 16,416, while the actual number after
decontamination was 15,035. Compared to the pangenome constructed using 567 strains, the
pangenome constructed using 977 samples increased in size by 2.58 Mb and added 647 genes. We found
that as the genome size increases, the pangenome size and the number of predicted genes also increase,
but the increase is relatively small, unlike in prokaryotes. It is evident that although the number of
genome samples increased by 410, the number of genes increased only slightly. Orthology inference
revealed that the A. flavus pangenome is composed of 15,628 protein-coding genes, which is 3,181
genes more than the reference genome of A.flavus NRRL3357 (GCA_009017415.1)25. These non-
redundant orthogroups could be subdivided into core (in all isolates, n = 9,584), accessory (in 5-95%
of the isolates, n = 5,085) and ‘unique’ (in <5% of the isolates, n = 959) genomes (Fig. 3a) after rigorous
removal of bacterial and other prokaryotic sequences by aligning the NR database. Here we need to
correct an analysis error in our previously submitted manuscript. Among them, the conserved core
genome accounts for 61.3%, the accessory genome accounts for 32.5%, and the unique genes account
for the remaining 6.2% of genes. The pangenome exhibits a closed trend as the population size increases
(Fig. 3b). Further results regarding the pangenome were updated in the manuscript.

homologues of 156 virulence genes….” What about the other strains? And were these homologues

Response: We thank the reviewers for their interest in this distribution. Among the 156 reported
virulence genes in Aspergillus fumigatus26, we identified 149 virulence genes present in the Aspergillus
flavus population through large-scale homology clustering using OrthoFinder27. After obtaining the
distribution matrix of virulence gene copy number distribution data matrix, we performed cluster
analysis and multiple group difference tests. The differential distribution of virulence gene copy number
among strains was determined by the Wilcox test between groups (P-value = 0.05). Overall, we found
the vast majority of the virulence genes (n=137, 137/149=92%) in both clinical and environmental
strains, and the phenomenon of homologues of virulence genes over-represented in clinical strains
versus environmental strains was not widespread(n=12, 12/149=8%). (Re_Figure 25a, and
Supplementary Material Figure S1 in the revised manuscript). It is true that a few virulence genes
have higher copy numbers in clinical strains than in environmental strains, for example, the homologues
virulence gene of Afu5g03790(Iron transport multicopper oxidase fetC in Aspergillus fumigatus) (Fig.
1a,d). In addtion, the homologue virulence gene of Afu8g00230(Chain A, Verruculogen synthase in
Aspergillus fumigatus Af293) is mainly distributed in W-Clade 2, mainly including environmental non-
aflatoxigenic clade strains (Fig. 1a in the revised manuscript). The distribution of the top 12 virulence
genes that differed in different subpopulations is shown in Re_Figure 25b.
